extracted.intended_audience: new and aspiring administrative law scholars (early-career legal academics and practitioners considering academia)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for early-career scholars and practitioners who want to enter or engage with the administrative law scholarly community, covering fellowships, publishing, presenting, following developments, and networking. Emphasizes concrete outlets, programs, and channels to amplify one’s voice in the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider part-time fellowship for practicing lawyers (ABA Administrative Law Fellowship)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you want to do fellowship while maintaining your current job, consider the ABA Administrative Law Fellowship launched earlier this year. The fellowship is a two-year program that pairs fellows with mentors in the legal academy and provides other support for entry into legal teaching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good option for practitioners who want to transition into the academic market while remaining employed; aimed to diversify legal academics in administrative law and regulatory practice. Contact Kevin Stack for questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pursue immersive full-time fellowships (e.g., ACUS Jerre S. Williams Fellowship)
rubrics_metrics.description: Full-time fellowships (six months to two years) such as the Jerre S. Williams Fellowship at the Administrative Conference of the United States (ACUS) are available for aspiring legal academics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages include working at a federal agency, interacting with agency officials and scholars, access to ACUS programming, and strong support for empirical/on-the-ground projects. Useful for immersive experience; author notes direct experience (did two studies for ACUS) and offers to discuss opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target top specialty journals in administrative law
rubrics_metrics.description: The two main specialty journals in administrative law are the Administrative Law Review (official law review of the ABA Administrative Law Section) and the Yale Journal on Regulation; both are premier journals with student editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These journals are primary outlets for traditional law review articles; they have online companions (Accord and Bulletin) for shorter pieces. Administrative Law Review also produces a podcast (A Hard Look).

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish shorter pieces and guest posts (Notice & Comment blog)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Notice and Comment blog publishes guest posts from administrative law scholars and experts about new articles or current developments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can submit guest posts or pitch ideas first; light editing is done on Notice & Comment. Symposia are hosted on the blog for books, developments, and articles—these are effective for engaging scholars and readers. Contact Emile Shehada or the author for help/pitches; submission information is linked on the blog.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pitch short articles to Administrative and Regulatory Law News (ARLN)
rubrics_metrics.description: ARLN is a quarterly magazine published by the ABA Administrative Law Section and distributed widely to Section members and on research platforms (Hein, Lexis, Westlaw).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider pitching short, practitioner-facing, or digestible pieces to ARLN for broad reach; contact Dan Walters (editor-in-chief) for pitches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write reviews and engage with others’ scholarship (Jotwell Administrative Law Section)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Administrative Law Section of Jotwell (Journal of Things We Like (Lots)) publishes reviews of articles and books and accepts guest contributors in addition to regular contributors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewing others’ work is an alternative way to develop and amplify your voice. Reach out to Miriam Seifter or the author if interested; you can subscribe to receive email versions of the reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish at The Regulatory Review for editorial feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: The Regulatory Review is an outlet that features scholarship and provides editorial support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike Notice & Comment's light editing, The Regulatory Review works with Penn law student editors who provide substantive and technical feedback—valuable for newer voices seeking editorial development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek to present at the ABA Administrative Law Conference
rubrics_metrics.description: The annual ABA Administrative Law Conference attracts academics, agency lawyers, and practitioners; it is a major networking and career-development venue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply to present (there is a spring call for panel proposals); ABA places a premium on new voices. In-person attendance maximizes networking; virtual format reduces networking opportunities but presentations remain important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present at centers, programs, and regular workshops
rubrics_metrics.description: Many centers and programs across the country host conferences and events on administrative law (e.g., C. Boyden Gray Center, Center for Progressive Reform, GW Regulatory Studies Program, Institute for Policy Integrity, Regulatory Transparency Project).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek out and present at these venues and at recurring workshops/series (e.g., Power in the Administrative State Workshop, Clubhouse Law and Governance) to get feedback, exposure, and networking within subfields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participate in Administrative Law New Scholarship Roundtable
rubrics_metrics.description: The Administrative Law New Scholarship Roundtable is a rotating, organized venue for aspiring and newer voices to present scholarship; hosts rotate among institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for calls for papers (typically late spring/early summer) and apply to present; organizers and rotating hosts provide structured feedback and peer engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow the field via curated digests and eJournals (Notice & Comment, Regulatory Review, SSRN)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stay current by subscribing to the Notice & Comment weekly digest, The Regulatory Review, and the SSRN U.S. Administrative Law eJournal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SSRN’s eJournal collects almost all new administrative law papers; when posting a draft to SSRN, manually select inclusion in the eJournal so the field sees it. SSRN also offers subject eJournals and a Comparative and Global Administrative Law eJournal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use program/career email digests (e.g., GW Regulation Digest)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many centers and programs produce regular email distributions that aggregate developments in the field; GW Regulatory Studies Regulation Digest is recommended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subscribe to these digests to get a weekly collection of updates and sources from multiple organizations, which helps monitor the field comprehensively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Join AALS Administrative Law Section and professor listservs
rubrics_metrics.description: The Administrative Law Section of AALS provides a supportive community, internal email listserv, programming at the annual AALS meeting (including a new voices workshop), and regular programming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Getting involved in the Section connects new scholars to peers and mentors; contact Kati Kovacs for involvement. Ed Richards moderates a long-standing administrative law professor email listserv—email him (or the author) to be added.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Twitter strategically to follow and learn from scholars
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter hosts many administrative law scholars; it is acceptable to consume without producing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Following scholars helps stay current and learn informal commentary and links; the author notes it’s fine to use Twitter passively. The author has a comprehensive follow list and offers follow/connection help via DM.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek mentorship, outreach, and peer feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Actively reach out to established scholars for mentorship, to share work, ask questions, and request introductions; small-group workshops and works-in-progress discussions are valuable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you lack an internal mentor, contact the author or others for introductions; offer to set up small-group Zoom workshops on works in progress, use senior scholars as sounding boards, and proactively solicit feedback and connections.
